extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers, cognitive scientists, and mathematicians interested in problem-solving heuristics and their applicability to AI
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze Polya's heuristic methods for mathematical problem solving and evaluate their relevance, limitations, and applicability to artificial intelligence, with special focus on auxiliary problems, learning, and problem-space representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's top goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya's principal aims are solving a general problem or proving a general theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the 'top goals' against which many of Polya's methods are framed; not all methods in Polya address these top goals directly (some target subproblems or pedagogical ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subgoals
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgoals exist in the main method, e.g., to test if a result is correct; to derive the same result in a different way; and to use the result to obtain a new problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each subgoal has its own specialized methods; they are still highly general methods. Recognize and evaluate subgoals as distinct moves in problem solving rather than mere auxiliary steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with a diversity of related (auxiliary) problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya pervasively uses related (auxiliary) problems as a path to the solution; about 50% of the basic questions in 'Devise a plan' and 60% of worked examples include at least one auxiliary problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auxiliary problems serve multiple roles — for their results, for their method, or to suggest further approaches. Examples: using the 2‑D triangle center-of-gravity problem as an auxiliary to the 3‑D tetrahedron; reducing a two-ship moving problem to the special case where one ship is at rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing for future problem solving (Examine the solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final step of every problem is to 'Examine the solution' with questions that extend beyond verification to using the present problem to provide methods, results, and lessons for future problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polya emphasizes learning from each solved problem (Descartes: 'Each problem that I solved became a rule which served afterwards to solve other problems'). Evaluate solutions for what they contribute to future problem-solving ability (building the solver's stock of problems and methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of inductions and analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya treats the credibility of analogies and inductions as qualitative and useful but resists reducing it to a quantitative calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He shows a correspondence between informal credibility judgments and the qualitative form of probability, but warns that attempts to apply probability calculus quantitatively to heuristic situations can lead to error. Evaluate analogical/inductive steps by qualitative plausibility, not naive numeric scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristics as rules of thumb within an integrated doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya's 'heuristic' refers both to an integrated body of doctrine and to individual rules of thumb; heuristics are useful but not guaranteed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess heuristics as parts of an integrated system (architecture + methods + principles about auxiliary problems and learning), not merely as isolated tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Work in letters not numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Work in letters not numbers." (Polya, 1945 p58)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer algebraic/symbolic formulations to concrete numeric instantiations because they enable general operations like finding special cases or applying to multiple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Treat symmetric elements symmetrically
rubrics_metrics.description: "Treat symmetric elements symmetrically." (Polya, 1945 p47)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit symmetry as a simplifying and organizing principle when modeling or transforming a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: If you can't construct a figure, construct one geometrically similar
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you can't construct a figure, construct one geometrically similar." (Polya, 1965 p9)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simpler or scaled analogues of the desired construction to gain insight; consider analogous smaller or simpler instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Check only 'touchy' parts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Check only 'touchy' parts of an argument." (Polya, 1945 p17)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus verification effort on vulnerable or non-obvious steps rather than rechecking every trivial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: If the unknown is a derivative, introduce derivatives generally
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the unknown is a derivative, then introduce derivatives generally." (Polya, 1945 p29)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the problem suggests a differential relationship, generalize the unknown to a family allowing broader manipulations and substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Two proofs are better than one
rubrics_metrics.description: "Two proofs are better, than one." (Polya, 1945 p60)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek alternative derivations — multiple independent solutions can confirm correctness and reveal deeper structure or generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Good problems grow in clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: "Good problems, like mushrooms, grow in clusters." (Polya, 1945 p64)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect productive problems to generate related variants and auxiliary problems; use clustering to expand useful problem collections for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Do not believe anything, but doubt only what is worth doubting
rubrics_metrics.description: "Do not believe anything, but doubt only what is worth doubting." (Polya, 1945 p197)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a pragmatic skepticism: concentrate critical scrutiny where it matters for the solution rather than universal doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Teachers should ask simple, general, unobtrusive questions from a short list
rubrics_metrics.description: "Teachers should ask questions that are simple, general, unobtrusive and from a short list." (Polya, 1945 p20)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogically prefer a small set of stereotyped, assimilable prompts so students internalize heuristic questioning and believe they could have thought of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: Ideas usable more than once become methods
rubrics_metrics.description: "An idea which can be used only once is a trick. If one can use it more than once it becomes a method." (Polya & Szego, 1924 p viii)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a tactic generalizes; favor reusable patterns that can be abstracted into methods over one-off clever moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality vs where 'the action' is (content-specific hidden steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a gap between Polya's general advice and the specific content-dependent 'hidden' steps that often determine success (e.g., noticing that 'some figures denote units and others tens' in a digits-sum impossibility proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether heuristics actually help reach key conceptual insights (the 'sagacity' or hidden trick) or mostly guide peripheral activity; measure applicability by whether they yield the decisive idea rather than just reduce flailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning emphasis: problems as building blocks for future problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya stresses that problems should be solved not only for their own sake but for what they contribute to future problem solving — methods, results, and problem instances expand the solver's competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate problem-solving processes on how well they add to a solver's 'stock' of problems and methods (in the paper: inner area vs rind metaphor — increase both area and perimeter of solvable problem space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six theses explaining limited impact on AI
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper enumerates six candidate theses for why Polya's heuristic has not impacted AI: (1) Polya's heuristic is irrelevant to AI (different aims); (2) human psychology is too different; (3) Polya's methods are either already known to AI or inapplicable; (4) the action is outside Polya's heuristic (need content-specific knowledge); (5) future-orientation (learning) is beyond current AI; (6) the diversity of auxiliary problems is beyond AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these theses as evaluation axes when judging the relevance of pedagogical heuristics to AI system design — test hypotheses about aim-alignment, psychological assumptions, novelty of methods, requirement for content knowledge, learning capabilities, and handling diverse auxiliary problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis 1: Polya's heuristic is not relevant (difference of aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya's work is oriented toward teaching problem solving (qualitative maxims) whereas AI aims toward precise formulations for constructing intelligent programs; this difference in aim may make Polya's advice inapplicable to AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mapping pedagogical heuristics to AI, evaluate whether the heuristic presupposes human abilities (e.g., rhetorical exhortation, motivation) or requires formalization that preserves utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis 2: Human psychology is too different
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya's heuristic is adapted to human psychological features (attention focusing, associative retrieval, motivation) that may have no counterpart or relevance in AI architectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge heuristics for dependence on human cognitive traits; high dependence suggests lower direct transferability to AI unless those cognitive functions are explicitly modeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis 3: Polya's methods are either known or inapplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of Polya's methods appear identical or similar to methods already used in AI; others may be inapplicable, and neither extreme plausibly explains the lack of impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalog which of Polya's methods have obvious AI analogues (e.g., substitution as operator selection) and which do not; use that mapping to determine novelty and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis 4: The action is outside Polya's heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya's general advice may be insufficient because the decisive moves in problem solving are highly content-specific (the 'hidden element' or key idea), and Polya's heuristics do not supply this detailed knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether adding Polya-style general heuristics to an AI system changes its ability to produce the decisive, content-rich insights, or merely improves peripheral search behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis 5: Future-orientation (learning) is still beyond AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya emphasizes learning from each problem to improve future problem solving; AI historically prioritized performance over learning, and current learning mechanisms may be inadequate to build the necessary stock of dispositions and problem instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess AI systems for their ability to assimilate solved instances into richer problem-solving competence (e.g., the CMU learning theorem prover example that assimilates theorems into future problem solving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis 6: Diversity of auxiliary problems is beyond AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary problems generated in the course of solving a main problem are extremely diverse in content and usage, and current AI systems cannot handle auxiliary problems in the rich manner Polya demonstrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test AI capability on generating, recognizing, and exploiting heterogeneous auxiliary problems (not only garden-variety symbolic manipulations but novel analogous or content-driven subproblems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem space model of problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem space consists of a set of states and operators that yield new states; problem solving is search in this space, modulated by heuristic knowledge about operators, paths, and models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate problem solvers by the problem spaces they can employ: the operators available, the quality of heuristic knowledge, and how effectively search is pruned or guided by that knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary problems as elements of problem spaces (reformulation thesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary problems can be viewed as elements in a problem space surrounding a main problem; the thesis reformulates as: 'Auxiliary problems require problem spaces that are still beyond AI's capability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the existing problem-space frameworks (states + operators) can represent the breadth of auxiliary problems Polya uses, especially the 'exotic' ones that are not mere symbolic-substitution subproblems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of concrete problem spaces (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete AI problem spaces (e.g., GEOMETRY THEORIST) demonstrate choices of states, operators (theorems), and heuristics (which theorems fit which figures); capabilities of a solver are expressed by the union of spaces it can work within.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use domain examples to judge whether an AI system's representation and operator repertoire suffice to capture the sort of auxiliary problem generation and use Polya documents (e.g., abstract geometry figures as states with theorems as operators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between garden-variety auxiliary problems and exotic auxiliaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Some substitutions and symbolic manipulations produce auxiliary problems that fit easily into AI's operator-selection view (garden-variety), while Polya also uses more 'exotic' auxiliary problems that do not fit so obviously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an AI's auxiliary-problem handling, distinguish performance on routine symbolic subproblems (likely solvable) from ability to generate and exploit novel, cross-domain, or structurally nonobvious auxiliaries (harder and more diagnostic).
